Chapter 1

London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black drizzle, with flakes of soot as big as full-grown snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun. Foot passengers, jostling one another’s umbrellas, and losing their foot-hold at street-corners where tens of thousands have been slipping and sliding since the day broke (if this day ever broke), add new deposits to the crust upon crust of mud, accumulating at compound interest.

Fog everywhere. Fog up the river; fog down the river; fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights; fog creeping into cabooses; fog lying on yards and hovering in rigging; fog drooping on gunwales; fog in the eyes and throats of ancient Greenwich pensioners and in the wrathful skipper’s pipe; fog about chance people on the bridges, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the misty clouds. Gas looming through it; shops lighted two hours before their time.

Rawest and densest near that leaden-headed old obstruction, Temple Bar; and hard by, in Lincoln’s Inn Hall, at the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in his High Court of Chancery. Never can there come fog too thick, nor mud too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition which this High Court of Chancery, most pestilent of hoary sinners, holds this day.

On such an afternoon the Chancellor ought to be—as here he is—softly fenced in with crimson cloth, addressed by a large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an interminable brief, contemplating the lantern in the roof where he can see nothing but fog; the bar ought to be—as here it is—tripping one another up on slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, making a pretence of equity, as players might; the solicitors ranged in a long matted well, with bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits, masters’ reports—mountains of costly nonsense—piled before them.

This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and blighted lands in every shire; its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard; its ruined suitor borrowing and begging through every man’s acquaintance; which so exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope—so overthrows the brain and breaks the heart—that there is not an honourable man among its practitioners who does not often give the warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here!”

Within the court: the registrar; maces and petty-bags; a little mad old woman in a squeezed bonnet with her “documents;” a sallow prisoner, come up again to purge his contempt, not likely ever to do it; and the ruined suitor from Shropshire, ready to cry “My Lord!” on the instant of rising.

Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. No man alive knows what it means; the parties least of all. Innumerable children have been born into it; innumerable young people married into it; innumerable old people died out of it. The little plaintiff promised a rocking-horse has trotted away into the other world; old Tom Jarndyce in despair blew his brains out at a coffee-house in Chancery Lane; but Jarndyce and Jarndyce still drags its dreary length before the court, perennially hopeless.

Jarndyce and Jarndyce has passed into a joke. That is the only good that has ever come of it. It has been death to many, but it is a joke in the profession; and when correcting Mr. Blowers, who said that such a thing might happen when the sky rained potatoes, the last Lord Chancellor observed, “or when we get through Jarndyce and Jarndyce, Mr. Blowers.”

How many people out of the suit it has spoiled and corrupted is a wide question; but in trickery, evasion, procrastination, spoliation, botheration, under false pretences of all sorts—down from master and receiver to copying-clerk—no man’s nature has been made better by it; shirking and sharking in all their many varieties have been sown broadcast by the ill-fated cause.

“Mr. Tangle,” says the Chancellor, latterly something restless.

“Mlud,” says Mr. Tangle—famous for Jarndyce and Jarndyce—“variety of points—feel it my duty tsubmit—ludship.”

“Several members of the bar are still to be heard, I believe?” Eighteen learned friends bob up like hammers, make eighteen bows, and drop into their places. “We will proceed with the hearing on Wednesday fortnight,” says the Chancellor; the question being only a question of costs, a mere bud on the forest tree of the parent suit.

“In reference,” proceeds the Chancellor, “to the young girl and boy, the two young people—whom I directed to be in attendance to-day—”

“Begludship’s pardon—dead,” interposes Mr. Tangle; “with their—grandfather.”

“Begludship’s pardon—victim of rash action—brains.”

A very little counsel with a terrific bass voice arises from the back settlements of the fog: “Will your lordship allow me? I appear for him. He is a cousin, several times removed. I am not at the moment prepared to inform the court in what exact remove he is a cousin, but he IS a cousin.”

The prisoner is sent back; the man from Shropshire is frowned into silence; the Chancellor dexterously vanishes; the empty court is locked up. If all the injustice it has committed and all the misery it has caused could only be locked up with it, and burnt in a great funeral pyre—why, so much the better for other parties than the parties in Jarndyce and Jarndyce!



Chapter 2

It is but a glimpse of the world of fashion that we want on this same miry afternoon. It is not so unlike the Court of Chancery but that we may pass from the one to the other; both are things of precedent and usage: oversleeping Rip Van Winkles, sleeping beauties whom the knight will wake one day.

It is not a large world. There is much good in it; it has its appointed place. But it is wrapped up in too much jeweller’s cotton and fine wool; it cannot hear the rushing of the larger worlds, nor see them as they circle round the sun. Its growth is sometimes unhealthy for want of air.

My Lady Dedlock has returned to her house in town for a few days previous to her departure for Paris—after which her movements are uncertain, as the fashionable intelligence—which, like the fiend, is omniscient of the past and present, but not the future—cannot yet undertake to say. She has been down at what she calls her “place” in Lincolnshire. The waters are out; an arch of the bridge has been sapped away; the low-lying ground is a stagnant river with melancholy trees for islands; the view from my Lady’s windows is alternately lead-coloured and in Indian ink. The vases on the terrace catch the rain all day, and the heavy drops fall—drip, drip, drip—upon the Ghost’s Walk all night. On Sundays the little church is mouldy; the oaken pulpit breaks out into a cold sweat; there is a general smell and taste as of the ancient Dedlocks in their graves. My Lady, looking in the early twilight from her boudoir at the keeper’s lodge—fire on the latticed panes, smoke from the chimney, a child running out to the wrapped-up man—has been put quite out of temper. My Lady says she has been “bored to death.”

Sir Leicester Dedlock is only a baronet, but there is no mightier baronet than he. His family is as old as the hills, and infinitely more respectable. He has a general opinion that the world might get on without hills but would be done up without Dedlocks. He would admit nature to be a good idea (a little low, perhaps, when not enclosed with a park-fence), but an idea dependent for its execution on your great county families. A gentleman of strict conscience, disdainful of all littleness, ready on the shortest notice to die any death rather than give occasion for the least impeachment of his integrity—an honourable, obstinate, truthful, high-spirited, intensely prejudiced, perfectly unreasonable man. Twenty years older than my Lady; a twist of the gout now and then; ceremonious, stately, most polite to her, with a gallantry that has never changed since he courted her.

He married her for love. A whisper goes that she had not even family; but she had beauty, pride, ambition, insolent resolve, and sense enough to portion out a legion of fine ladies. Wealth and station, added to these, soon floated her upward; for years now she has been at the centre of the fashionable intelligence and at the top of the fashionable tree. Having conquered her world, she fell into the freezing mood: an exhausted composure, a worn-out placidity—perfectly well-bred; if translated to heaven to-morrow, she might be expected to ascend without any rapture.

With all her perfections on her head, my Lady has come up to town; and at her house, upon this muddy, murky afternoon, presents himself an old-fashioned old gentleman, attorney-at-law and eke solicitor of the High Court of Chancery—Mr. Tulkinghorn. Rusty to look at, reputed rich; surrounded by a halo of family confidences; of the old school; knee-breeches tied with ribbons, stockings that never shine; mute, close; found speechless but at home at corners of dinner-tables in great houses, where everybody knows him and half the Peerage stops to say, “How do you do, Mr. Tulkinghorn?”—salutations he receives with gravity and buries along with the rest of his knowledge. There are noble mausoleums rooted for centuries in retired glades of parks among the timber and the fern, which perhaps hold fewer noble secrets than walk abroad among men, shut up in the breast of Mr. Tulkinghorn.

My Lady supposes herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her knows her weaknesses and can turn her and her whole troop; who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience, lead them, and, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,” say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest place.”

“My Lady’s cause has been again before the Chancellor, has it, Mr. Tulkinghorn?” says Sir Leicester.

“Yes. It has been on again to-day,” replies Mr. Tulkinghorn, bowing to my Lady, who shades her face with a hand-screen.

“It would be useless to ask,” says my Lady with Lincolnshire dreariness upon her, “whether anything has been done.”

“Nothing that YOU would call anything,” replies Mr. Tulkinghorn.

“Nor ever will be,” says my Lady.

Sir Leicester has no objection to an interminable Chancery suit. It is a slow, expensive, British, constitutional kind of thing; to complain of it were to encourage some person in the lower classes to rise up somewhere—like Wat Tyler.

“As a few fresh affidavits have been put upon the file,” says Mr. Tulkinghorn, “and as I see you are going to Paris, I have brought them in my pocket.” He puts on his spectacles and begins, “‘In Chancery. Between John Jarndyce—’”

My Lady interrupts, desiring him to miss as many of the formal horrors as he can. The fire is hot; the hand-screen is beautiful and small. My Lady, changing her position, looks nearer at the papers—nearer still—asks, impulsively, “Who copied that?”

“Is it what you people call law-hand?” she adds, toying with her screen.

“Not quite,” says Mr. Tulkinghorn, examining it. “Probably the legal character was acquired after the original hand was formed. Why do you ask?”

“Anything to vary this detestable monotony. Oh, go on, do!”

He reads again. The heat is greater; my Lady screens her face. Sir Leicester starts and cries, “Eh? What do you say?” for Mr. Tulkinghorn had risen hastily. “I am afraid,” says he, “that Lady Dedlock is ill.”

“Faint,” my Lady murmurs with white lips, “only that; but it is like the faintness of death. Don’t speak to me. Ring, and take me to my room!”

Bells ring; feet patter; silence ensues. Mercury at last begs Mr. Tulkinghorn to return.

“Better now,” quoth Sir Leicester, motioning him to sit and read to him alone. “I have been quite alarmed. I never knew my Lady swoon before. But the weather is extremely trying, and she really has been bored to death down at our place in Lincolnshire.”
